answer.rationale: Two of the three current problems are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing it can move both with one slot. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifted SMB first-week activation) point the same direction, and memory_91's activation messaging is a narrower downstream lever that depends on users reaching the product at all. Promotional pricing is the tempting response to the competitor, but memory_73 is the one inherited record that still carries its numbers: +31% trial starts and +18% quarterly revenue bought with +12pp renewal churn concentrated in small accounts — exactly the price-sensitive SMB segment under attack. That trades long-term qualified revenue for a quarter of headline growth and is disqualified by the primary objective. Referral incentive (memory_57) is sound but addresses established customers, not the acute top-of-funnel bleed; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) targets a segment not currently in decline. I want the two archived onboarding/signup records because both are consolidated summaries that assert lifts without stating whether the lift was in activation only or in retained, qualified revenue, and without stating segment or sample size. The specific downstream risk: stripping signup fields and onboarding steps can raise completion while lowering lead quality — more accounts activate, fewer qualify, and the harm shows up a quarter later in renewals, the same shape as memory_73's failure mode. So I run at standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, hold out a control, and instrument downstream qualification and 90-day retention as primary guardrails rather than judging on completion rate alone. If the archive shows either memory measured only proximal activation, I narrow to a small guarded test.
